pos: n. (the western principality of Britain, whose Reformation came by the Welsh Bible of 1588 and whose awakening came by field preaching)
etymology: Old English Wealas, the foreigners, from Proto-Germanic walhaz, a Roman or a Celt; the Welsh call their own country Cymru, the land of fellow-countrymen.
biblical_def: Wales is the western principality of Britain, and its history is the plainest case in these islands of a nation reformed by having the Scriptures put into its own tongue. The old British church held the western hills after the Saxon settlement and kept its own reckoning of Easter until the Synod of Whitby, and Augustine of Canterbury could not bring its bishops to terms. Union with England came by statute in 1536, and with it a policy that treated Welsh as a barbarism to be worn away. Against that policy Parliament passed in 1563 an act requiring the Bible and the Book of Common Prayer in Welsh. William Salesbury gave the New Testament in 1567 and Richard Davies laboured with him; William Morgan gave the whole Bible in 1588, and that book, more than any council or any prince, made a Welsh Protestant people. Rhys Prichard put doctrine into verse that labourers could carry in the head. Under the Commonwealth Vavasor Powell and Walter Cradock preached through the country, and John Penry had already died at Westminster in 1593 for pressing the want of preaching in Wales. Then Griffith Jones set up his circulating schools, teaching the poor to read the Welsh Bible, and out of that reading came Howell Harris, Daniel Rowland and William Williams. The dictionary records Wales as a nation to whom God gave the Word in its own language.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a principality as the territory of a prince; a tongue as the language of a nation; a version as a translation; vernacular as native to the country of one's birth; and a revival as renewed attention to religion.
webster_full: PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; the territory of a prince, or the country which gives title to a prince.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; hence, speech; language; the whole sum of words used by a nation.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of rendering into another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as a man's vernacular tongue.
REVIVAL, n. Return or recall to life; renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
corruption_summary: Western principality made Protestant by the Welsh Bible of 1588 and awakened by the circulating schools and the Calvinistic Methodist preachers, against both an English policy that would have extinguished the language and a modern reading that makes the result merely cultural.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet over Wales and the dictionary names both. The first is the Tudor and Hanoverian policy that treated Welsh as a barbarous speech to be worn out of the people, leaving parishes to be served in a tongue the parishioners did not have; against it stands the apostolic wonder that men heard “how hear we every man in our own tongue” (Act 2:8), and Paul's plain rule that an unintelligible service is speech thrown away, for “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken” (1Co 14:9). The act of 1563 and Morgan's Bible of 1588 are therefore not concessions to sentiment but obedience to Scripture.

The second corruption is modern and runs the other way. It reads Welsh nonconformity as essentially a movement of national feeling that happened to wear a religious dress, so that chapel, hymn and revival become expressions of identity rather than effects of the preached Word. The record will not bear it. What changed Wales was reading: Griffith Jones taught the poor their letters so that they could read one book, and the men converted at those desks preached. Nehemiah's pattern is the Welsh pattern, where they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8), and Paul's question is the Welsh question, “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). A nation is not awakened by pride in itself.

Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget, to be born; “wherein we were born”, Acts 2:8.

“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — Griffith Jones's circulating schools.
“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — John Penry's complaint, for which he died in 1593.

pos: n. (the mountain princedom of north Wales, seat of the see of Bangor and the last Welsh power to fall to Edward I)
etymology: Welsh Gwynedd, probably from the same root as the Irish Féni, the Goidelic settlers; the Latin form is Venedotia.
biblical_def: Gwynedd is the north-western princedom of Wales, holding Snowdonia and the coastal plain behind it, and its mountains made it the last Welsh power to be reduced. Its princes claimed descent from Cunedda; Rhodri Mawr, Llywelyn ap Iorwerth and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd ruled from Aberffraw and Dolwyddelan, and the independence of native Wales ended with Llywelyn's death in 1282 and the castles Edward I raised at Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech. The see of Bangor, founded by Deiniol in the sixth century, is the ecclesiastical centre; its cathedral was burned more than once in the wars and rebuilt poorly, and the diocese was among the poorest in the kingdom, so that its parishes were commonly held by absentees and served by curates who could barely live. That poverty is the key to the Reformation's slow progress in the north: the Welsh Bible of 1588 was law, but a book needs a reader and a preacher needs a stipend. The change came late and came from below, through the schools and then through the Calvinistic Methodist exhorters; Thomas Charles of Bala, in the old Gwynedd country, organised the supply of Welsh Bibles, and John Elias preached across Anglesey and Caernarfonshire with great effect. The dictionary records the mountains as a shelter and refuses to make them a merit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mountain as a large mass of earth rising above the common level; a see as the seat of episcopal power; a curate as one employed to perform the duties of another; a fastness as a stronghold; and a stipend as a settled pay.
webster_full: MOUNTAIN, n. A large mass of earth and rock, rising above the common level of the earth or of adjacent land.
SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; the diocese or jurisdiction of a bishop.
CURATE, n. A clergyman employed to perform the duties of another; one who has the cure of souls.
FASTNESS, n. A strong hold; a fortress or fort; a place of defence difficult of access.
STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
scriptures: As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Mic 6:9
The LORD'S voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it.
corruption_summary: North Welsh princedom whose mountains preserved a native power until 1282 and whose poor see of Bangor left the Reformation to be carried by schools and preachers rather than by endowment.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the trust men put in a strong country. Gwynedd was defensible, and its defensibility bred a confidence that outlasted the thing defended; the hills held off armies for eight centuries and could not hold off one judgment. Scripture allows the comfort and relocates it: the mountains are a figure of the LORD's own keeping, for “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people” (Psa 125:2), and the only fastness that cannot be taken is a name, since “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). Caernarfon was built precisely to prove that rock is not refuge.

A second and quieter corruption belongs to the dictionary's own side of the account, and is named as ours. A reformed establishment held the see of Bangor for two centuries while leaving it too poor to be preached in, filling it with men who drew the title elsewhere and left the cure to a curate; the promise God makes is of “pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15), and a diocese administered as a source of revenue has not received them. The rod spoke before the remedy came, for the LORD's “voice crieth unto the city” (Mic 6:9), and the remedy, when it came, came through Bala and the schools and not through the bishops.

“pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15) — the want of them in the poor see of Bangor.

pos: n. (the middle kingdom of Wales, the march country between Gwynedd and England, long contested and early opened to the English Reformation)
etymology: Welsh Powys, from Latin pagenses, the country people or dwellers in the open land, in contrast with the mountain districts.
biblical_def: Powys is the middle kingdom of Wales, the open and fertile country between the mountains of Gwynedd and the English shires, and its name means the people of the plain. Because it was open it was fought over: Offa drew his dyke along its eastern edge, the kings of Mercia pressed it, and its princes were as often allied with England against Gwynedd as with Gwynedd against England. It was divided in the twelfth century into Powys Fadog in the north and Powys Wenwynwyn in the south, and the division made it weaker still. Its openness had one effect the Reformation turned to account. Lying next to Shrewsbury and Ludlow and crossed by the drovers' roads, Powys received English preaching and English books earlier than the western coasts, and the Welsh New Testament of 1567 and the Bible of 1588 travelled those same roads. Walter Cradock, a Monmouthshire man, itinerated through the borders in the sixteen-thirties and was silenced for it; Vavasor Powell, born at Knucklas in Radnorshire, made the mid-Wales uplands his circuit and was imprisoned repeatedly after the Restoration. The dictionary records Powys as border country in both senses, and holds that a frontier is a place of passage for the gospel before it is a place of defence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a march as a border or frontier of a country; a dyke as a mound or bank; itinerant as travelling from place to place; to repair as to restore after injury; and a path as a way beaten by the feet.
webster_full: MARCH, n. A border; a frontier; the boundary of a country or territory; usually in the plural, as the marches of Wales.
DYKE, n. A ditch; a mound of earth or stone raised as a boundary or to resist water.
ITINERANT, a. Passing or travelling about a country; wandering; not settled; as an itinerant preacher.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, waste or injury; to mend.
PATH, n. A way beaten or trodden by the feet of man or beast; a track; a narrow way.
scriptures: By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Neh 4:17
They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.
corruption_summary: The open middle kingdom of Wales, pressed by Mercia and divided against itself, whose border roads carried English books and itinerant preachers into mid-Wales earlier than the coasts received them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name here is the border mind, which judges every neighbour by the frontier and comes to think of its own safety as the first article of religion. Powys divided itself to keep itself and halved its strength; its princes bargained now with Mercia and now with Gwynedd, and the bargaining produced no lasting peace for either half. Scripture puts the health of a town where men do not look for it, in the character of its inhabitants, for “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked” (Pro 11:11). A march is not made secure by its dyke.

The second word belongs to the eighteenth century, when the border roads that had carried the Reformation in carried indifference after it, and whole uplands kept a form of worship with no preaching in it. The call then is not to invent something but to go back and look: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16), with the warning attached that the men addressed answered, We will not walk therein. The promise held out to those who do is the promise of Isaiah, that they shall be called “The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isa 58:12), and the manner of the work is Nehemiah's, every man with one hand on the wall and one on a weapon (Neh 4:17).

Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, a gap in a wall; “The repairer of the breach”, Isaiah 58:12.

“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — the drovers' roads that carried the Welsh Bible.
“The repairer of the breach” (Isa 58:12) — Vavasor Powell itinerating the mid-Wales uplands.

pos: n. (the southern Welsh county of the Vale and the coalfield, seat of the see of Llandaff and the ground of the first Welsh field preaching)
etymology: Welsh Gwlad Morgan, the land of Morgan, from a tenth-century ruler of the district; anglicised as Glamorgan.
biblical_def: Glamorgan is the southern Welsh county, holding the fertile Vale along the coast, the uplands behind it and the valleys that were later cut open for iron and coal. The see of Llandaff stands in it, and so do the old Cistercian houses of Margam and Neath, dissolved with the rest in the sixteen-thirties of the previous century's reckoning; the county's gentry took the abbey lands and with them a settled interest in the Reformation. Its importance to the dictionary is that Glamorgan is where Welsh field preaching began in earnest. Howell Harris of Trevecca, converted in 1735, carried his exhorting west and south; Daniel Rowland came over from Cardiganshire; and the Calvinistic Methodist societies multiplied through the Vale and the hill parishes faster than any parish church could hold them. When the ironworks at Merthyr and Dowlais and then the coal of the Rhondda drew tens of thousands into the valleys, the chapels went with them, and the industrial population of south Wales was evangelised as it was gathered. The harvest figure is the right one for the county and the labourers were few. The dictionary records Glamorgan as a place where the Word went out to men at their work, and where the going out was done by preachers the establishment had not sent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vale as a tract of low ground between hills; a mine as a pit from which minerals are taken; harvest as the season of gathering; a labourer as one who works; and to itinerate as to travel from place to place.
webster_full: VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
MINE, n. A pit or excavation in the earth, from which metals, coal and other mineral substances are taken.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn gathered.
LABOURER, n. One who labours in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill.
ITINERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.
scriptures: Deu 8:9
A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Ecc 5:9
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field.
corruption_summary: Southern Welsh county of the Vale, the see of Llandaff and the coalfield, where Howell Harris and Daniel Rowland began the field preaching that gathered the industrial valleys the parish system could not hold.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the county invites is the identifying of plenty with blessing. Glamorgan was a land whose stones were iron, and the promise of Deuteronomy sounds almost like a description of it, “a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass” (Deu 8:9); but the promise is attached to a covenant and followed in that chapter by the warning not to forget the God who gave it. The valleys produced wealth and they consumed men, and the chapels that were built over the pitheads were built in the knowledge that “the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9) and that the men who raise the profit are not therefore served themselves.

The second word is against the parish order of the eighteenth century, and the dictionary speaks it plainly because the order was its own. A settled ministry that would not go to where the people had moved left the harvest standing, and the exhorters who went were irregular men without orders or licence. Our Lord's own account of the case is that “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and the apostolic precedent for preaching done by the unordained scattered is express, for “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). An establishment that answers such preaching with prosecution has mistaken the disorder for the disease.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad as seed; “they that were scattered abroad”, Acts 8:4.

Hebrew sadeh (H7704) — a field, open country; “the king himself is served by the field”, Ecclesiastes 5:9.

“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — the valleys outgrowing the parishes.
“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — Harris and Rowland without licence.

pos: n. (the island county off north-west Wales, ancient seat of the druids and later a stronghold of Welsh Calvinistic Methodism)
etymology: Old Norse Ongulsey, Ongul's island; the Welsh name is Mān, and the island was called Mān mam Cymru, Anglesey the mother of Wales, for its corn.
biblical_def: Anglesey is the island lying off the north-west corner of Wales across the Menai strait, flat and fertile where the mainland is mountainous, and called in Welsh the mother of Wales because its corn fed Gwynedd. It was the last stronghold of the druids in Britain, and Tacitus records the Roman army crossing the strait in the year 60 and cutting down the groves in which the island's sacrifices were performed. After the conversion of Wales it held the shrine of Cybi at Holyhead and a great number of small churches, and after the fall of Gwynedd it passed with the rest to the crown. Its place in the dictionary belongs to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Calvinistic Methodist cause took deep hold on the island, and John Elias, born at Abererch and settled at Llanfechell and then Llangefni, preached there for forty years with an authority that made him the leading man of the Welsh connexion; Christmas Evans, the Baptist, held Anglesey as his field from 1791 and planted preaching stations across it. The destruction of the groves and the planting of the chapels are the two events the dictionary sets side by side.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water; a grove as a cluster of trees; a druid as a priest of the ancient Celts; corn as grain; and a connexion as a body of persons united.
webster_full: ISLE, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; an island.
GROVE, n. A cluster of trees of no great extent; in Scripture, trees planted and consecrated to idolatrous worship.
DRUID, n. A priest or minister of religion among the ancient Celtic nations of Gaul, Britain and Germany.
CORN, n. A single seed of certain plants; in collective use, grain of all kinds, as wheat, rye, barley and oats.
CONNEXION, n. The act of joining, or state of being joined; a body of persons associated or united.
scriptures: Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof.
Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
Isa 49:1
Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The LORD hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name.
Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
corruption_summary: Fertile island county off north-west Wales, the last British seat of the druids whose groves Rome cut down in the year 60, and from the seventeen-nineties the field of John Elias and Christmas Evans.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern recovery of druidry as native wisdom unjustly suppressed, a piece of antiquarian invention that became a religion. The groves on Anglesey were not a school of philosophy but a place of sacrifice, and the dictionary declines to soften the account. Scripture's own precedent for what to do with the apparatus of such a religion is the burning at Ephesus, where “Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19) — and it is worth marking that there the owners burned them, which is the only clean way such a fire is lit. What Rome did on the island in the year 60 was a judgment and not a conversion.

The second word is a word of promise rather than of rebuke, and it is the island's own. Isaiah twice sends the praise of God out to the islands, bidding men sing “his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof” (Isa 42:10), and opening a prophecy with “Listen, O isles, unto me” (Isa 49:1). Anglesey heard it late. When John Elias preached at Llangefni and Christmas Evans gathered his stations, an island that had been the last refuge of the groves became a place where “the multitude of isles be glad” (Psa 97:1) was something more than a figure.

Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, to hearken, to obey; “Listen, O isles, unto me”, Isaiah 49:1.
Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ears, to attend closely; “and hearken, ye people, from far”, Isaiah 49:1.
Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, to be glad; “let the multitude of isles be glad”, Psalm 97:1.
Greek periergos (G4021) — busy about trifles, hence magical, curious arts; “which used curious arts”, Acts 19:19.
usage: “the isles, and the inhabitants thereof” (Isa 42:10) — Mān, the mother of Wales.
“which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them” (Act 19:19) — the groves cut down in the year 60.
“let the multitude of isles be glad” (Psa 97:1) — John Elias at Llangefni.

pos: n. (the south-western Welsh county and its castle, holding the shrine of St Davids and the English-speaking district called Little England beyond Wales)
etymology: Welsh Penfro, the end of the land, from pen, a head, and bro, a region; anglicised as Pembroke.
biblical_def: Pembroke is the county at the south-western end of Wales, and its name means land's end. Norman and Flemish settlement in the twelfth century planted a lowland of English speech across its southern half, marked off from the Welsh north of the county by the line still called the Landsker, so that the district was known as Little England beyond Wales. The castle at Pembroke was the strongest in the march, and Henry Tudor was born in it in 1457. In the north of the county stands St Davids, the shrine of the patron of Wales and the chief pilgrimage of the Welsh church, where two journeys were reckoned the equal of one to Rome; the cathedral sits in a hollow by the sea, out of sight of raiders. The county was a landing place as well as a departure: Henry Tudor came ashore at Mill Bay in 1485, and in the Civil War Pembroke town held for Parliament in a royalist country and was besieged by Cromwell in 1648. The dictionary records the shrine and refuses the traffic in it, and marks the sea as the county's highway. A place at the end of the land is a place of embarkation, and Scripture gives the pilgrim no permanent address.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shrine as a case for sacred relics; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; a haven as a harbour; a promontory as a headland; and a sojourner as one who dwells for a time.
webster_full: SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; applied to the tomb of a saint, visited by devotees.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to a relic or shrine.
HAVEN, n. A harbour; a port; a bay or inlet of the sea, where ships can ride in safety.
PROMONTORY, n. A high point of land or rock projecting into the sea beyond the line of the coast; a headland.
SOJOURNER, n. One who dwells in a place for a time; a temporary resident; a stranger.
scriptures: Isa 60:9

Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the LORD thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee.
They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
corruption_summary: South-western Welsh county of the Landsker and the castle where Henry Tudor was born, holding the shrine of St Davids whose double pilgrimage was reckoned the equal of one to Rome.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the pilgrimage itself, and the dictionary names it as traffic. St Davids drew the Welsh for centuries on the published reckoning that two journeys there counted as one to Rome, which is a tariff and not a devotion; the shrine was stripped at the Reformation and the relics removed, and the dictionary counts that a mercy to the pilgrims. What the New Testament leaves the traveller is not a holy place but a holy direction, for “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). A cathedral set in a hollow to be hidden from raiders is a fair emblem of a religion that had to be guarded; Christ's city is the reverse, for “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).

The second word is for the sea, which was this county's road. Pembrokeshire men went down to the sea in ships as a matter of livelihood, and Scripture speaks of them as such: “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23), the psalm that goes on to show them at the end of their resources crying to the LORD. Isaiah makes the ships of the nations the carriers of a better freight, when “the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far” (Isa 60:9). The county that watched for raiders and for claimants to a throne is given a watch worth keeping.
roots_summary: Greek polis (G4172), a city; Greek meno (G3306), to abide or continue; Hebrew 'oniyah (H591), a ship.
roots_lines: Greek polis (G4172) — a city, a walled town; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.
Greek meno (G3306) — to remain, to abide, to continue; “no continuing city, but we seek one to come”, Hebrews 13:14.
Greek oros (G3735) — a mountain, a hill; “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid”, Matthew 5:14.
Hebrew 'oniyah (H591) — a ship; “They that go down to the sea in ships”, Psalm 107:23.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; “Surely the isles shall wait for me”, Isaiah 60:9.
usage: “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — the double pilgrimage to St Davids.
“A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14) — a cathedral built in a hollow to be hidden.
“They that go down to the sea in ships” (Psa 107:23) — the county's highway and livelihood.

pos: n. (the oldest Welsh town and its county, ground of Griffith Jones's circulating schools and of the Welsh Bible's first readers)
etymology: Welsh Caerfyrddin, the fort of Myrddin, from caer, a fort, and the personal name; the Roman station was Moridunum, the sea fort.
biblical_def: Carmarthen is the county town of south-west Wales and reckoned the oldest town in the country, standing on the Towy where the Romans had a station and an amphitheatre. Its county is the one in which the Welsh learned to read. Griffith Jones, rector of Llanddowror in Carmarthenshire from 1716, found that his people could not read the Bible that had been law since 1588 and set about the want with a method rather than a lament: a schoolmaster with no building would come to a parish for three months in the slack of the agricultural year, teach children and adults together to read Welsh and the catechism, and then move on. These were the circulating schools, and by Jones's death in 1761 something near a hundred and sixty thousand people had passed through them in a country of perhaps half a million. Peter Williams of Llandyfaelog, converted under Whitefield, produced the annotated Welsh Bible that went into Welsh houses in quantity; and the Presbyterian academy at Carmarthen trained ministers for the dissenting congregations, though it drifted to Arianism in the eighteenth century and had to be answered. The dictionary records Carmarthenshire as the place where catechising and reading were made the ordinary work of the parish.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to catechise as to instruct by question and answer; a school as a place of instruction; precept as a command or rule; to train as to teach and form by practice; and literacy's root, to read, as to peruse written words.
webster_full: CATECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers; to instruct in the principles of religion.
SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
PRECEPT, n. Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; a maxim; a doctrine.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach and form by practice; as to train up a child.
READ, v.t. To utter or go over the words of a writing; to peruse; to learn by observation.
scriptures: And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
corruption_summary: Oldest Welsh town and its county, where Griffith Jones of Llanddowror put perhaps a hundred and sixty thousand Welsh people through circulating schools so that they could read the Bible of 1588.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that catechising is ordinary pastoral work and that literacy is a means of grace's outward administration, not a secular preliminary to it. Griffith Jones did not treat reading as a civic improvement that might later be turned to religious use; he taught reading in order that the Welsh might have the holy scriptures in the hand, on the ground that Timothy “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15). The schools taught the catechism alongside the letters, and the Welsh marginal reading at Proverbs 22:6 is Catechise, so that “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) was understood in Carmarthenshire as a direction about doctrine and not merely about manners.

The method is worth naming because the modern instinct runs against it. Jones's schools were slow, repetitive and unambitious in each visit, taking three months in one parish and then beginning again in the next, which is exactly the prophet's description of how instruction actually lands: “precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isa 28:10). Where the county went wrong it went wrong at the top. The Presbyterian academy in the town, founded to train preachers, moved toward Arianism in the middle of the eighteenth century, and the dictionary records that as a failure of its own dissenting side: an academy that loses the beginning of wisdom has nothing to teach, for “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).
roots_summary: Greek sophizo (G4679), to make wise; Hebrew chanak (H2596), to train up; Hebrew tsav (H6673), a precept.
roots_lines: Greek sophizo (G4679) — to make wise, to instruct; “are able to make thee wise unto salvation”, 2 Timothy 3:15.
Greek hieros (G2413) — sacred, holy; “thou hast known the holy scriptures”, 2 Timothy 3:15.
Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train, to dedicate, to catechise; “Train up a child in the way he should go”, Proverbs 22:6.
Hebrew tsav (H6673) — an injunction, a precept; “precept must be upon precept”, Isaiah 28:10.
Hebrew yir'ah (H3374) — fear, reverence; “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”, Proverbs 9:10.
usage: “thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — the end for which the circulating schools taught reading.
“precept must be upon precept” (Isa 28:10) — three months in a parish, then the next.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — the Carmarthen academy's drift to Arianism.

pos: n. (the mid-Welsh county town and its county, holding Trevecca, the family seat of Howell Harris and the cradle of the Welsh revival of 1735)
etymology: Welsh Aberhonddu, the mouth of the Honddu; the English Brecon is from Brycheiniog, the land of Brychan, a fifth-century ruler.
biblical_def: Brecon is the county town of Brycheiniog in mid-Wales, standing where the Honddu meets the Usk under the high moorland of the Beacons. It had a Benedictine priory that became the parish church and later the cathedral of a new diocese, and a grammar school refounded in the sixteenth century. Its standing in the dictionary rests on one farm. Trevecca, in the parish of Talgarth in Breconshire, was the home of Howell Harris, who was converted at Talgarth church at Whitsun 1735 while receiving the Lord's Supper and began almost at once to exhort his neighbours house by house. Harris was never ordained; he was refused orders four times, and his work was therefore irregular from the start, carried on in houses, barns and open fields and organised into societies with appointed exhorters over them. The same year and without knowledge of him, Daniel Rowland was awakened in Cardiganshire; the two met in 1737, and the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist movement dates from their joining. Harris later gathered a community at Trevecca and the Countess of Huntingdon placed her college there in 1768. The dictionary records Brecon as the ground where a layman began what the bishops had declined to commission.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to revive as to return to life or vigour; to exhort as to incite by words; a society as a number of persons united; a beacon as a signal fire on a height; and refreshing as the act of reviving.
webster_full: REVIVE, v.t. To return to life; to recover new life or vigour; to be reanimated after apparent death.
EXHORT, v.t. To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge to any good action, especially to the practice of virtue and piety.
SOCIETY, n. A number of persons united, either for mutual benefit, or for the promotion of a particular object.
BEACON, n. A signal erected on an eminence, consisting of a pitch barrel or fire, to notice the approach of an enemy.
REFRESHING, n. The act of refreshing; relief after fatigue or suffering; new vigour or animation.
scriptures: Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hab 3:2
O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.
Act 3:19
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
Isa 44:3
For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:
corruption_summary: Mid-Welsh county town under the Beacons, holding Trevecca where Howell Harris was converted in 1735 and began the unordained exhorting out of which Welsh Calvinistic Methodism grew.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern manufacture of revival, the assumption that what happened at Talgarth and Llangeitho can be arranged by method, atmosphere and sufficient expectation. The Welsh awakening began with two men in two counties who did not know of each other, and the dictionary holds that this is the ordinary shape of the thing. Scripture asks for it as a gift and not as a technique: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6), and Habakkuk prays “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years” (Hab 3:2) with the plea for mercy in wrath attached, which is not the language of a man expecting to produce an effect.

The second word is against the opposite error, which is the one the establishment fell into here. Harris was refused ordination four times, and the refusal did not stop the work; it only guaranteed that the work would be done outside the parish structure and would eventually leave it. Where repentance and conversion are preached the refreshing follows, for “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” (Act 3:19), and the promise of the poured-out Spirit is made to the thirsty and the dry rather than to the regular: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3). A church that will not commission its converted men should not be surprised to find them gone.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah (H2421), to live or revive; Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn or be converted; Greek anapsuxis (G403), refreshing.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to keep alive, to revive; “Wilt thou not revive us again”, Psalm 85:6.
Hebrew po'al (H6467) — a work, a deed; “revive thy work in the midst of the years”, Habakkuk 3:2.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; “Repent ye therefore, and be converted”, Acts 3:19.
Greek anapsuxis (G403) — a cooling, a recovery of breath, refreshing; “the times of refreshing shall come”, Acts 3:19.
Hebrew yatsaq (H3332) — to pour out, to pour forth; “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty”, Isaiah 44:3.
usage: “Wilt thou not revive us again” (Psa 85:6) — Talgarth and Llangeitho in the same year, unknown to each other.
“the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” (Act 3:19) — Harris exhorting house by house.
“floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3) — orders refused four times and the work going on.

pos: n. (the ancient Welsh see on the Taff, proverbially the poorest and worst-served diocese in the kingdom)
etymology: Welsh Llandaf, the church on the Taff, from llan, an enclosure or church, and the river name.
biblical_def: Llandaff is the Welsh see standing on the Taff above Cardiff, and one of the four ancient dioceses of Wales. Its traditional founder is Dyfrig, its patron Teilo, and its cartulary, the Book of Llandaff, was compiled in the twelfth century under Bishop Urban partly to assert the see's claims against St Davids and Hereford. The cathedral was rebuilt from Urban's time and enlarged in the thirteenth century. What the dictionary records is the condition of the diocese afterward. Llandaff was reckoned the poorest see in England and Wales, and for that reason it was treated as a stepping place: its bishops commonly held it with another preferment and lived elsewhere, and in the eighteenth century Richard Watson held it for over thirty years from the Lake District and visited his diocese scarcely at all. The cathedral itself fell into ruin, so that by the seventeen-twenties the nave stood roofless and a plain classical temple had been built inside the ruins to hold the services; the whole was restored only in the nineteenth century. Meanwhile the Calvinistic Methodists and the Baptists filled the Glamorgan valleys with chapels. The dictionary names an absentee episcopate as a failure of shepherding and does not soften the charge because the shepherds were Protestant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a diocese as the circuit of a bishop's jurisdiction; a shepherd as one who tends sheep; an overseer as one who superintends; absentee as one who withdraws from his station; and preferment as advancement to a place of honour or profit.
webster_full: DIOCESE, n. The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; the district in which a bishop exercises his office.
SHEPHERD, n. One who has the care of sheep; in a figurative sense, a pastor or minister of the gospel.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; in Scripture, a bishop or pastor of a church.
ABSENTEE, n. One who absents himself from his country, office, post or duty; a landholder living away from his estate.
PREFERMENT, n. Advancement to a higher office or dignity; a superior place or office; promotion.
scriptures: Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Jer 23:1
Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! saith the LORD.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Ancient Welsh see on the Taff, reckoned the poorest in the kingdom and so held in plurality by absentees, its cathedral roofless by the seventeen-twenties while the Glamorgan valleys filled with chapels.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is ours, and the dictionary names it without mitigation. A reformed church held Llandaff for three centuries and governed it as a source of income. Bishops kept the title and the revenue and lived in England; the cure was left to curates on a few pounds a year; the cathedral stood open to the weather while a temple was raised inside its ruins to keep the services dry. Ezekiel's indictment was written for exactly this and requires no adjustment: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). Jeremiah adds the consequence, which is dispersal: “Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture” (Jer 23:1). The chapels of the valleys were, in part, the scattering.

The second paragraph names the standard that was abandoned, because the remedy is not a new office but the old one performed. Peter's charge to elders sets the motive against the very abuse Llandaff displayed: feed the flock “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). Paul's charge at Miletus grounds the duty in the price paid for the flock, bidding overseers “feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). A diocese is not a benefice to be drawn upon from a distance, and poverty is a reason for residence rather than an excuse for absence. The dictionary holds that where episcopacy was defended on apostolic grounds it was bound to be exercised on apostolic terms.

roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7462) — to pasture, to tend, to shepherd; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?”, Ezekiel 34:2.
Hebrew hoy (H1945) — an exclamation of woe; “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel”, Ezekiel 34:2.
Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, to disperse; “that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture”, Jeremiah 23:1.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed; “Feed the flock of God which is among you”, 1 Peter 5:2.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop; “the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers”, Acts 20:28.
usage: “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2) — a see held for thirty years from the Lake District.
“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the poorest diocese treated as a stepping place.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — the price that makes absence inexcusable.

pos: n. (the Shropshire castle town that was the seat of the Council in the Marches of Wales, the court through which Wales was governed for a century and a half)
etymology: Old English hlūde hlāw, the hill by the loud water, from hlūd, loud, and hlāw, a hill or mound.
biblical_def: Ludlow is the Shropshire town above the Teme, built round a Norman castle that became the administrative capital of Wales. The Council in the Marches of Wales sat there from the late fifteenth century, given statutory footing under Henry VIII and presided over by a Lord President; it exercised both judicial and executive power over Wales and the border shires, and for a century and a half the ordinary Welshman's experience of royal government was a summons to Ludlow. Prince Arthur kept court there and died there in 1502; Mary Tudor was sent there as a child. The council was abolished in 1689. Two things in its record concern the dictionary. The first is that its jurisdiction, being prerogative rather than common law, was a standing grievance: it fined, imprisoned and bound over on its own authority, and the Long Parliament struck at it along with Star Chamber. The second is that Richard Baxter, as a youth, was placed in the household of the council's chaplain at Ludlow and saw the court at close quarters, and recorded in his own account the looseness of the place. The dictionary holds the magistrate's office to be of God and its abuse to be judged by the same word that establishes it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly for consultation; a magistrate as a public civil officer; prerogative as an exclusive privilege; jurisdiction as legal authority; and justice as the giving to every man his due.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
PREROGATIVE, n. An exclusive or peculiar privilege; an antecedent and exclusive right.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.
JUSTICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every man what is his due; conformity to the law.
scriptures: Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: Shropshire castle town and seat of the Council in the Marches of Wales, a prerogative court that governed Wales for a century and a half until the Long Parliament struck at its jurisdiction.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the prerogative court, a tribunal deriving its power from the sovereign's will rather than from law, and the dictionary names it as a corruption of the magistrate's office and not as its mere excess. Scripture gives the magistrate a sword and gives it to him for a defined end: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). A minister of God with a commission has a rule to answer to; a court that makes its own rule as it goes has the sword without the commission. The consequence is the one Solomon states, that the character of rulers is felt in the mood of a whole people, for “when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).

The second word is against the other error, which is to conclude from the abuse that the office is worthless. The dictionary does not take the step. What is required of the man who holds the sword is stated and it is not complicated: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The measure of a government is not its efficiency in reducing a province but the righteousness by which it is itself governed, since “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). Richard Baxter, set down in that household as a boy, drew from it a lifelong distrust of courts and a lifelong insistence that rulers are under law; the dictionary reckons both lessons sound.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, a minister; “he is the minister of God, a revenger”, Romans 13:4.
Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword, the instrument of civil execution; “he beareth not the sword in vain”, Romans 13:4.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, a verdict; “but to do justly, and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.
Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; “Righteousness exalteth a nation”, Proverbs 14:34.

“when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2) — a summons to Ludlow as the ordinary face of government.
“Righteousness exalteth a nation” (Pro 14:34) — Baxter's judgment on the household he was placed in.
